questions.question: What does 'problem-model fit' assess?
options: Which specific LLM provider offers the cheapest pricing
Whether a given problem's characteristics genuinely match what LLM-based approaches are good at, before committing to build one
How many GPUs are needed to train a model
Whether a model's context window is large enough
questions.explanation: Problem-model fit is an upfront assessment of whether a problem is actually well-suited to an LLM-based solution, before deciding which model or architecture to use.

questions.question: Why is calculating an exact monthly invoice total considered a poor fit for an LLM-based solution?
options: LLMs cannot process numbers at all
It requires perfect, deterministic accuracy and already has a simple, well-established deterministic solution, making an LLM's probabilistic nature an unnecessary risk
Invoices are too short for an LLM to process
This is actually a great fit for an LLM-based solution
questions.explanation: Invoice calculation needs zero tolerance for error and has a straightforward deterministic formula already available, making a probabilistic LLM approach both riskier and less efficient than a simple calculation.

questions.question: A team wants to add AI to a feature that simply validates whether a submitted form field matches a required format. Which question best evaluates this proposal?
options: Should we approve it since AI can be added to any feature?
Does this problem require perfect, deterministic accuracy, and does a simpler, well-established deterministic solution (like a format check) already exist?
Which specific model should we use for this?
How much context window will this feature need?
questions.explanation: This is a classic poor-fit signal: format validation is deterministic and already well-solved by simple rule-based logic, so the problem-model fit question should be asked before any model selection discussion happens.
